key_insight: CoReMem treats memory for coding agents as an investment: information worth retaining should save enough future effort to justify the cost of writing and reading it. It also considers when an agent should use available memory as a new task unfolds.
problem_solved: Coding agents working through successive tasks must preserve useful knowledge about an evolving repository before knowing the next task, without letting memory overhead outweigh its benefits.
method: Introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a framework that accounts for both memory-writing and memory-reading costs.
Use prospective valuation to weigh potential future usefulness when choosing what to remember for unknown upcoming tasks.
Guide actor adaptation around when consulting and acting on stored memory can save effort during task execution.
impact: The framework offers practitioners a way to reason about memory efficiency, rather than simply retaining more information. The provided abstract is truncated, so empirical gains and evaluation details cannot be assessed.
visual_elements: Timeline of successive coding tasks on an evolving repository, with memory passed between tasks.
Balance scale contrasting expected future effort saved against memory-writing and memory-reading costs.
Decision flowchart: retain information, encounter a new task, then decide whether to use memory.
Memory-card icons distinguishing potentially useful repository knowledge from costly, low-value notes.
paper_title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
paper_authors: Peiwen Li, Harshit Verma, Sophia Zhou, Haiwen Wang, Ngoc Bui
